newsitem.title: USA: T-bond yld may hit 7.20 if March jobs top 200,000.
newsitem.headline: T-bond yld may hit 7.20 if March jobs top 200,000.

text.p: If nonfarm payrolls growth exceeded 200,000 last month, coupled with rising hourly wages, Treasury bond yields could march quickly to 7.20 percent and begin a trek toward 7.35, market strategists said.

"Any number in the 200,000 range -- even though it would be weaker than the average over the last few months -- still suggests the Federal Reserve would (tighten credit) one more time, and that's what's going to bother the market," said Cary Leahey, senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.

The Labor Department will release the March employment report on Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Economists in a Reuters survey expected, on average, 182,000 new jobs were created in the month compared to a whopping 339,000 in February.
Jobs growth has averaged 272,000 in the December through February period and 209,000 over the last six months.

Meanwhile, the unemployment rate was expected to drop a notch to 5.2 percent, which would mark its lowest reading since October. Experts said a dip in the jobless rate to 5.1 percent or below would wreak havoc on Treasury prices.

Leahey said financial markets expect payrolls growth of less than 200,000. But he said any increase in wages of 0.4 or 0.5 percent versus the previous month would be "very negative," adding that such a jump would "wash out" any market-friendly figures in the report.
Economists in the Reuters poll predicted wages would leap 0.4 percent in March against a 0.2-percent rise in February.

"If we get over 250,000 (payrolls) and if wages are up 0.4 percent, we'll see a bounce to 7.20 percent (on the long bond yield) in two to three seconds," Leahey added, pointing to a roadblock at 7.20 percent, and a cushion below at 6.97.

Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist for fixed income at Credit Suisse First Boston, said he was focusing particularly on wages and the jobless rate. Yet overall, Alexy said data on March retail sales due later this month should attract more attention than the long-awaited monthly employment report.

"Demand is really the focus," Alexy said, alluding to a statement last week that accompanied the central bank's first interest rate hike in more than two years. "Now that the Fed is in motion, the market is going to think any (report) that isn't in line brings us to another policy action."
In its statement, the Fed said it raised rates "in light of persistent strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances."
Alexy said evidence that inflation is percolating beneath the economy's surface would "knock the market down for the count," and bond yields could leap to 7-3/8 or 7.50 percent over a period of days.

Still, the Credit Suisse First Boston strategist said he expected a mere 133,000 new jobs to have been created in the month, a 5.3 percent jobless rate, and a 0.2 percent uptick on average hourly earnings.
Alexy called his forecasts "safe" for the Treasury market that, if on target, would keep bond yields confined to the 7.07- to 7.11-percent range.
